slides.say: p, q, r and s are prime numbers, and p is smaller than q, which is smaller than r, which is smaller than s. Given: z is equal to p to the power of s, times q to the power of r. Which of the following necessarily divides z?
A hard one, all letters. But underneath, it's a factor question. What is z built from? [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, understanding with the letters, and then the same idea with numbers.
[short pause] Our first method. z is p to the power of s, times q to the power of r. So z contains the prime p, s times, and the prime q, r times. And nothing else.
at: So z contains the prime p

slides.say: Now careful, a lot of students see r and s in z, and think they're factors of z. They're not. They're only exponents, they count how many times p and q appear. The primes r and s themselves aren't inside z at all.
at: see r and s in z

slides.say: And remember the check. A power of a prime divides z only if z has that prime at least as many times.
Choice number one, r. r isn't a factor of z, so it's out. Choice number four, s to the power of q. There's no s in z at all. Out.
Choice number three, q to the power of s. It needs s copies of q. z has q only r times, and r is smaller than s. Not enough q's, out.

Three are out, so in the exam you'd circle choice number two. Here, let's see why it works. p to the power of r needs r copies of p. z has s of them, and r is smaller than s, so there are enough. q to the power of q needs q copies of q. z has r of them, and q is smaller than r, so enough again. So choice number two is our answer.
at: p to the power of r
So choice number two is our answer

slides.say: [pause] Our second method, plugging in numbers. When the primes are letters, plug in the smallest primes, in the right order. Why the smallest? Any primes in that order fit the givens, and small ones are the easiest to work with. So p is two, q is three, r is five, and s is seven.
Then z is two to the power of seven, times three to the power of five. Seven twos and five threes.
Choice number one, r is five. z is built only from twos and threes, so five doesn't divide it. Out.
Choice number two, p to the power of r times q to the power of q, is two to the power of five, times three cubed. Five twos, and z has seven. Three threes, and z has five. It fits.
Can I circle it already? No. I'm plugging in numbers, so it might work only for these numbers. I have to knock out the other two first.

Choice number three, q to the power of s, is three to the power of seven. Seven threes, and z has only five. Out. Choice number four, s to the power of q, is seven cubed, and there's no seven in z at all. Out. So choice number two. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
